title: Resolvents and Yosida regularization
subtitle: Bounded approximants for generators and self-adjoint operators
adaptation: Mathematical companion outlining the definitions, argument, worked cases, and scope of the source lecture.

slides.title: A bounded substitute for an unbounded map
slides.lead: Begin with a closed operator on a Hilbert space. Its domain may be smaller than the whole space.
body: The resolvent solves a shifted equation on that domain. A bounded inverse lets us study an unbounded generator using ordinary bounded operators.

slides.title: What dissipativity contributes
slides.lead: A dissipative generator cannot instantaneously increase squared norm.
body: Taking a real inner product with a solution to the shifted equation gives a lower estimate. The range condition is still required to make the inverse everywhere defined.

slides.title: From resolvent to contraction
slides.lead: Multiplication by the positive shift creates a bounded contraction.
body: The inverse solves the domain problem, and the resolvent inequality gives the norm bound. A shifted resolvent is the building block of the classical approximant.

slides.title: The classical Yosida approximant
slides.lead: The bounded generator shares the dissipativity of the original one.
body: Form the difference between the resolvent contraction and the identity. For each fixed positive lambda it acts on every vector, unlike G.

slides.title: Convergence is a domain statement
slides.lead: The original action is recovered on legal domain vectors.
body: For x in the domain of G, the resolvent identity gives both statements directly. Strong convergence of J extends from the dense domain by uniform boundedness.
slides.mathtex: J_\lambda x-x=R_\lambda Gx,\quad G_\lambda x=J_\lambda Gx\to Gx

slides.title: Diagonal example: rates capped by lambda
slides.lead: Let G multiply the n-th coordinate by negative n.
body: The approximant caps the size of arbitrarily fast decay rates: it is bounded for each lambda, but its n-th eigenvalue converges to -n for each fixed n.

slides.title: Why the domain matters
slides.lead: Square summability of a sequence is not the same as square summability after multiplying by n.
body: For x_n=1/n^2 the generator is defined, whereas for x_n=1/n it is not. Every bounded G_lambda still acts on both sequences. This does not establish convergence to Gx outside the domain.

slides.title: Symmetric approximation for self-adjoint A
slides.lead: Unitary evolution calls for a real, symmetric spectral cutoff.
body: The bounded scalar function fixes any finite spectral value asymptotically while suppressing the tails symmetrically. It produces a bounded self-adjoint operator.

slides.title: The symmetric formula is resolvent-based
slides.lead: The two imaginary shifts combine to give the same bounded spectral function.
body: Because the terms are conjugate on the real line, their sum is real. The pair of imaginary resolvents is the self-adjoint counterpart to the positive real resolvent used for dissipative generators.

slides.title: The exact convergence claim
slides.lead: Strong convergence on D(A) is sufficient to recover the original action.
body: Norm convergence cannot approach an unbounded operator. The right theorem states that the bounded approximants recover Ax for each x on which A is defined.
slides.takeaway: Two resolvent constructions serve related but different dynamics.
